title: Number of tablets for a prescribed dose
blurb: Work out how many tablets make one prescribed dose, check it makes sense, and type it the way Pearson marks it.
question: A person is prescribed furosemide 80 mg. The tablets in stock contain furosemide 40 mg each. How many tablets should be given?

teach.body: Formal rule: number of tablets = dose prescribed ÷ strength of one tablet, with both in the same unit. Plain English: how many of these tablets add up to the dose on the chart? The prescription is what you WANT; the tablet strength on the box is what you HAVE. Want goes on top. On Part A this is one of the four oral items, and the answer goes into a number-only box with "tablet(s)" printed after it.
teach.cite: Pearson VUE NMC practice papers; NMC ToC test specification (oral medications)

teach.caption: Five steps every time, even when the numbers look easy.

teach.h: Worked example: Mr Price on a cardiology ward
teach.body: Daniel Price, 64, is prescribed furosemide 80 mg in the morning. The box says furosemide 40 mg tablets. Want 80 mg, have 40 mg. Units match. 80 ÷ 40 = 2. Sense-check: each tablet is half the dose, so two tablets make the whole dose. In the exam you type 2 into the box; "tablet(s)" is already printed after it.

teach.caption: Decimals do not change the method. Use the on-screen calculator for 7.5 ÷ 2.5 if you need to.

teach.h: Right way up vs upside down
teach.caption: Multiply your answer by the tablet strength: it must give back the prescribed dose.

teach.text: Inverting the fraction: dividing what you HAVE by what you WANT (40 ÷ 80 = 0.5) instead of want ÷ have (80 ÷ 40 = 2). If the prescribed dose is bigger than one tablet, the answer must be more than 1.

teach.body: Tablet items use a number-only box with "tablet(s)" printed after it. Type digits only: 2, not "2 tablets" and not 2.0. Pearson marks trailing zeros as a format risk and the box rejects letters. Read the stem once more for a frequency: "80 mg twice a day" still asks for one dose unless the question asks for a daily total.
teach.cite: Pearson VUE NMC practice tests, answer-format guidance

items: Tablets = dose prescribed (want) ÷ strength of one tablet (have).
Units must match before you divide.
Sense-check: answer × strength = prescribed dose; usually 0.5 to 4 tablets.
Classic error: have ÷ want (inverted) gives a fraction when the dose is bigger than one tablet.
Type the number only into a "tablet(s)" box, with no trailing zero.

summary: You can now calculate the number of tablets for any prescribed dose using want ÷ have, with matched units. You can also sense-check the result against the tablet strength and type it in Pearson's number-only format.

A.q: A person is prescribed amlodipine 10 mg. The tablets available contain amlodipine 5 mg each. How many tablets should be given?
A.why: Want ÷ have = 10 mg ÷ 5 mg = 2 tablets. Check: 2 × 5 mg = 10 mg.

whyNot.0: This is have ÷ want (5 ÷ 10), the inverted fraction. It gives 2.5 mg, a quarter of the dose.
whyNot.2: This doubles the correct answer as if the dose were given twice; the stem asks for one dose.
whyNot.3: This misreads 5 mg as 0.5 mg, a tenfold slip: 20 tablets would give 100 mg.

A.q: A patient is prescribed metformin 1 g. Each tablet contains metformin 500 mg. How many tablets should be given?
A.why: Convert first: 1 g = 1000 mg. Want ÷ have = 1000 mg ÷ 500 mg = 2 tablets.

whyNot.0: This is have ÷ want, the inverted fraction (500 ÷ 1000).
whyNot.1: This misreads the strength as 50 mg (a tenfold slip), giving 20.
whyNot.2: This adds the 1 g to the 500 mg before dividing; 1 g is the whole dose.

A.q: A client is prescribed sodium valproate 600 mg. The tablets available contain sodium valproate 200 mg each. How many tablets should be given?
A.why: Want ÷ have = 600 mg ÷ 200 mg = 3 tablets. Check: 3 × 200 mg = 600 mg.

whyNot.1: This doubles the dose as if it were for a whole day at twice a day; the stem asks for one dose.
whyNot.2: This is have ÷ want (200 ÷ 600), the inverted fraction.
whyNot.3: This misreads 200 mg as 20 mg, a tenfold slip giving 30.

B.q: A woman is prescribed labetalol 300 mg. The stock tablets contain labetalol 100 mg each. How many tablets should be given?
B.why: Want ÷ have = 300 mg ÷ 100 mg = 3 tablets. Three 100 mg tablets make 300 mg.

whyNot.0: Inverted: 100 ÷ 300 gives a third of a tablet, only 33 mg.
whyNot.1: This divides by 200 mg, a strength not on the label.
whyNot.3: This multiplies the single dose by three as if three doses were asked for.

B.q: A service user is prescribed bisoprolol 7.5 mg. The tablets available contain bisoprolol 2.5 mg each. How many tablets should be given?
B.why: Want ÷ have = 7.5 mg ÷ 2.5 mg = 3 tablets. Check: 3 × 2.5 mg = 7.5 mg.

whyNot.1: This divides by 5 mg instead of 2.5 mg, giving 1.5.
whyNot.2: This drops the decimal point in 7.5 mg (a tenfold error), giving 30.
whyNot.3: This is have ÷ want, the inverted fraction.

B.q: A person is prescribed bendroflumethiazide 5 mg. Each tablet contains bendroflumethiazide 2.5 mg. How many tablets should be given?
B.why: Want ÷ have = 5 mg ÷ 2.5 mg = 2 tablets. Check: 2 × 2.5 mg = 5 mg.

whyNot.0: This is have ÷ want, the inverted fraction (2.5 ÷ 5).
whyNot.1: This misreads 2.5 mg as 0.25 mg, a tenfold slip giving 20.
whyNot.2: This doubles the answer as if two doses were asked for.

C.q: A person is prescribed levetiracetam 750 mg twice a day. The tablets available contain levetiracetam 250 mg each. How many tablets should be given for each dose?
C.why: One dose is 750 mg. Want ÷ have = 750 mg ÷ 250 mg = 3 tablets per dose. Twice a day is the frequency, not part of the single-dose sum.

whyNot.0: This is the daily total (two doses of 3), but the question asks for each dose.
whyNot.2: This is have ÷ want, the inverted fraction.
whyNot.3: This divides by 500 mg instead of the 250 mg on the label.

C.q: A patient is prescribed sertraline 150 mg. Sertraline 50 mg tablets and sertraline 100 mg tablets are both in stock. Using one strength only, what is the fewest number of tablets that gives the dose?
C.why: 100 mg tablets cannot make 150 mg in whole tablets (150 ÷ 100 = 1.5). The 50 mg tablets give 150 ÷ 50 = 3 tablets exactly.

whyNot.0: 1.5 of a 100 mg tablet; the stem gives no scoring, so a half tablet is not allowed.
whyNot.1: Two tablets would need one of each strength; the question says one strength only.
whyNot.3: This doubles the correct count, as if two doses were asked for.

C.q: A woman is prescribed nifedipine modified-release 40 mg. The pharmacy has supplied nifedipine modified-release 10 mg tablets. How many tablets should be given?
C.why: Want ÷ have = 40 mg ÷ 10 mg = 4 tablets. Four is at the top of the usual range, so check the box strength and the prescription before giving.

whyNot.1: This is have ÷ want, the inverted fraction (10 ÷ 40).
whyNot.2: This divides by 20 mg, a strength not supplied.
whyNot.3: This misreads 10 mg as 1 mg, a tenfold slip giving 40.

reteach.title: Put the prescription on top
reteach.question: A person is prescribed 60 mg and each tablet contains 30 mg. Which number goes on top of the fraction?

blocks.body: The prescription tells you what the person must receive, so it always sits on top: want ÷ have. 60 mg wanted from 30 mg tablets is 60 ÷ 30 = 2 tablets. If you put 30 on top you get 0.5, which would give only 15 mg.

blocks.h: Say it as you type it

blocks.text: If your answer times the tablet strength does not equal the prescribed dose, you have inverted the fraction or misread a strength.

explain.body: WANT is the dose on the prescription. HAVE is the strength of ONE tablet on the box or label, not the pack size (for example "28 tablets").

test.q: A person is prescribed propranolol 80 mg. The box reads "Propranolol 40 mg, 28 tablets". How many tablets should be given?
test.why: HAVE is 40 mg per tablet (28 is the pack size). 80 mg ÷ 40 mg = 2 tablets.

whyNot.0: This divides by the pack size (28 tablets) instead of the strength, giving 2.86.
whyNot.1: This is have ÷ want, the inverted fraction.
whyNot.2: This multiplies by the pack size; 56 tablets would be the whole box twice over.

test.q: A patient is prescribed gliclazide 120 mg. Each tablet contains gliclazide 40 mg. How many tablets should be given?
test.why: Want ÷ have = 120 mg ÷ 40 mg = 3 tablets. Check: 3 × 40 mg = 120 mg.

whyNot.0: Inverted fraction: have ÷ want gives a third of a tablet.
whyNot.2: This divides by 80 mg, not the 40 mg on the label.
whyNot.3: This doubles the dose as if it were given twice.

explain.body: A strength such as 2.5 mg or 0.5 mg does not change anything. Divide want by have on the calculator and check the answer is a sensible number of tablets.

test.q: A person is prescribed lorazepam 1.5 mg. The tablets available contain lorazepam 0.5 mg each. How many tablets should be given?
test.why: Want ÷ have = 1.5 mg ÷ 0.5 mg = 3 tablets. Check: 3 × 0.5 mg = 1.5 mg.

whyNot.1: This misreads 0.5 mg as 5 mg, a tenfold slip.
whyNot.3: This divides by 1 mg, a strength not stated.

items.label: tablets: a unit or decimal error

test.q: A person is prescribed carbamazepine 400 mg. Each tablet contains carbamazepine 100 mg. How many tablets should be given?
test.why: Want ÷ have = 400 mg ÷ 100 mg = 4 tablets. That is the top of the usual range, so it is worth a second check of the label.

whyNot.1: This misreads 100 mg as 10 mg, a tenfold error giving 40 tablets.
whyNot.3: This divides by 200 mg, not the 100 mg on the label.
